event: The French National Assembly grants Jews full citizenship — the civic-assimilation path opens. Over the following eight decades emancipation extends across Western and Central Europe; Reform Judaism and religion-only self-definition (Hermann Cohen's Judentum) build its institutional vehicle.
mechanism: Legal emancipation; the alternative's constituency is the large Western/Central European Jewish strata
src: Framework §3 typology (constituency: France post-1791); corpus: Meyer, Mendes-Flohr
note: Opening marker for the alternative whose closure occupies Stage 1. The European-Jewish self-identification thread (emancipation-squeeze framework) carries the fuller record.

event: Burckhardt documents the regional governance baseline: Tiberias Jews pay kharaj and paid "heavy fines" under Jezzar; the Jewish banking family running Acre's finances is mutilated in service; non-Muslim security is conditional at every level.
quote: there is scarcely an instance in the modern history of Syria, of a Christian or Jew having long enjoyed the power or riches which he may have acquired: these persons are always taken off in the moment of their greatest apparent glory.
mechanism: Toleration within structural subordination: kharaj, fines, mutilation, office-at-sufferance
src: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (1822), pp. 180, 321–327
note: Swiss Protestant eyewitness, 1810–12. One of four independent primary witnesses (with Schwarz, Finn, Mishaqa) to the same structural pattern. Also attests continuous Jewish presence in all four holy cities, ~1,000 Jews in Tiberias alone.

event: Hebron is stormed by Ibrahim Pasha and given to his soldiers for several days during the suppression of the fellahin revolt; five Jews purposely murdered, the community stripped. Mechanism is Egyptian-soldier license, not a fellahin attack — the Jews "could not be viewed as rebels" and were sacked anyway.
quote: five Jews were purposely murdered, and all their property which had not been buried under ground was either stolen or destroyed in the most wanton and cruel manner… the whole Jewish community was sunk into poverty.
mechanism: Soldier-license sack of a neutral community at a breakdown of order; promised protection not delivered
src: Schwarz, Descriptive Geography (1850), pp. 398–399 — resident eyewitness
note: A guard was posted "but it was too late." The 1834 Safed plunder in the same revolt is carried in the defense-decoupling ledger.

event: Damascus Affair: ritual-murder prosecution of prominent Damascus Jews under Egyptian transitional rule, with French-consular instigation. Mishaqa — the forensic investigator personally assigned to the remains — attests the defendants' innocence and the torture that produced confessions.
quote: I can state with certainty that the prominent Jews who were imprisoned in this case were innocent… After severe tortures they confessed, except for Musa al-Salanikli, who maintained his innocence even though he was more cruelly tortured than the rest.
mechanism: Minority security contingent on the external-power configuration of the moment
src: Mishaqa, Murder, Mayhem, Pillage, and Plunder (Thackston tr. 1988), pp. 193–200; Frankel, The Damascus Affair (1997)
note: Not an Ottoman-tolerance case: it occurred under Egyptian rule with French-Catholic instigation, and the restored Ottoman state issued a corrective response (Frankel). Mishaqa also confirms human remains were found — his account rejects the ritual-murder framing while complicating a pure-fabrication narrative.

event: Hebron's Jews — neutral in the clan war — are plundered, beaten and wounded when the Pasha of Jerusalem reinstates Abd al-Rachman by force; the community's president is then made to sign (and pay for) a certificate that no harm was done. Consular pressure to protect them fails.
quote: The Jews of Hebron had been grossly ill-used, beaten, and wounded; one old man had his hand shot off… But there was one of the managers to whom it was impossible to subscribe this lying certificate… because it had been shot away by the infuriated assailants.
actor: Pasha of Jerusalem's soldiery; Abd al-Rachman's strongman regime
mechanism: Extraction under factional warfare; consular protection attempted and defeated
src: Schwarz, Descriptive Geography (1850), Appendix 16, pp. 430–432
note: Shows the post-1838 consular regime already operating — and failing — eight years before Finn's tenure documents it working.

event: British Consul Finn records that Jerusalem's Jews are secure only because an external guarantor stands behind them: the local order produces the abuse, the consulate provides the remedy.
quote: They were no longer outwardly persecuted — being well known to be under British protection.
mechanism: Security via withdrawable external protection, not via the local governance system
src: Finn, Stirring Times (1878), p. 56 — consular primary
note: The load-bearing sentence for the external-guarantor dependency that Section 9 of the framework generalizes: every non-sovereign arrangement rested on a guarantor that could be withdrawn.

event: Damascus massacre of Christians — Mishaqa's first-hand Arabic account documents mass killing of a dhimmi community whose consular-protected rise was experienced as a violation of the established order. Lewis: 19th-century dhimmi equality itself was read as "a violation of the old established principles of the dhimma."
quote: What remained of Muslim tolerance was subjected to severe strains as the dhimmīs tried to combine the totally incompatible objectives of equal citizenship, foreign protection, and national independence. (Lewis, p. 170)
actor: Damascus mob; authorities (Mishaqa: "planned by the authorities")
mechanism: Mass violence when the subordination order is perceived as violated — the 1860 Christian analog of 1929
src: Mishaqa (Thackston tr. 1988); Lewis, The Jews of Islam, p. 170
note: If equality was experienced as violation, sovereignty was an order-of-magnitude greater disruption — the structural core of the framework's Section 9 (nation-state as regional anomaly).

event: Moses Hess, Rome and Jerusalem: the assimilation alternative is diagnosed as failing from inside its own tradition — the host society is reclassifying Jews from religion to race, sixteen years before the word "antisemitism" exists.
quote: The Germans hate less the Jewish religion than they hate their race… Neither religious reform nor baptism, neither Enlightenment nor Emancipation will open the gates of social life before the Jews.
mechanism: Racial reclassification defeats the religion-only retraction; legal emancipation cannot deliver social emancipation
src: Hess, Rome and Jerusalem (1862), quoted in Avineri, Moses Hess (1985)
note: The diagnostic precedes the catastrophe by 80 years — evidence the closure was visible on internal evidence, not retrospectively re-read after the Holocaust.

event: Wilhelm Marr coins "Antisemitismus": racial reclassification of Jews becomes an organized political movement in Germany, then Austria and France (Dreyfus affair 1894).
mechanism: Social closure by racial category — conversion, reform, and patriotism cease to purchase acceptance
src: Framework §2–3 (Hess 1862 diagnosis; Marr 1879 coined the term); corpus: Efron, Hart ed.

event: Pogrom wave across the Russian Pale after the assassination of Alexander II; the May Laws follow in 1882. Mass Jewish emigration westward begins — the dominant response is exit toward America, not Palestine.
mechanism: State-tolerated violence plus legal restriction launch the forty-year emigration stream
src: Alroey, An Unpromising Land (2014), ch. 1; framework stage 1
note: The First Aliyah (~25–35K, 1882–1903) is a small side-stream of this flow, with 50–60% onward/return migration (yerida).

event: Dispersed emigration operates as the dominant Jewish alternative: ~2.5 million Eastern European Jews emigrate before 1914 — overwhelmingly to the United States, ~6% to Palestine.
actor: Eastern European Jewish migrants; HIAS/ICA channels
mechanism: US/UK/Argentina/Brazil/South Africa channels absorb the refugee stream; Palestine is a marginal destination
src: Alroey, An Unpromising Land (2014), ch. 1, p. 35
note: This is the alternative whose staged legal closure (1924 → 1938 → 1939 → 1940–48) later channels a majority-refugee population to Palestine.

event: Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation, written out of the pogrom year: civil rights obtained by law do not produce social acceptance — the racial reclassification holds even for the "man of culture."
quote: The legal emancipation of the Jews is the crowning achievement of our century. But legal emancipation is not social emancipation.
mechanism: Same mechanism as Hess 1862, restated from inside the Russian experience
src: Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation (1882), in Road to Freedom (Maccoby tr., 1944)

event: Ottoman policy prohibits Jewish settlement in Palestine and moves to strip foreign Jews' right under the 1867 Land Code to acquire land; by the 1890s Jewish immigrants are "absolutely prohibited" from settling in the relevant vilayets — while Muslim in-migration (Circassian, Bosnian, Algerian, Egyptian) into the same zones is permitted or directed.
quote: all Jews, Ottoman and foreign, should be prohibited from settling in Palestine, and… foreign Jews should lose their right under the 1867 Land Code to acquire land.
mechanism: Religion-gated settlement and land law — the demographic baseline of 1947 was itself an asymmetric legal product
src: Mandel, The Arabs and Zionism Before World War I (1976), pp. ~180, ~270 — Ottoman archival
note: Symmetric-rigor row: the "they had not consented to mass immigration" steelman claim, applied to Jewish but not to contemporaneous Muslim immigration, does not survive symmetric application (framework §7 qualification). The cap also tracked imperial weakness twice over: the strong 16th-century empire had absorbed the entire Sephardi expulsion (Salonika a Jewish-plurality city), while the weak 19th-century one — its finances under the European-run Public Debt Administration from 1881, the very year of the first restrictions — rationed entries it could not enforce. Capitulations shielded foreign-subject Jews from deportation, baksheesh dissolved the rest, and on the order of 60,000 entered against standing policy by 1914 (Mandel documents the enforcement failure).

event: Petah Tikva riot: colony farmers confiscate the donkeys of neighboring fellahin "even though the fellahin were apparently innocent"; the ensuing riot is labeled a pogrom by the Zionist press. Yishuv-side provocation is documented at the very start of the settlement record.
quote: the violent riot by fellahin in Petah Tikvah in late March 1886… was in actual fact the outcome of overbearing behavior on the part of the farmers in the colony.
mechanism: Symmetric-rigor row: early Yishuv–Arab violence was bidirectional, and this instance began with the colonists
src: Shapira, Land and Power (1992), p. 57
note: Held against any one-directional reading of the early violence record; the same ledger carries the Arab-initiated record with the same rigor.

event: Ahad Ha-Am, "Slavery in Freedom": Western emancipation's internal price named from inside — spiritual slavery under the veil of outward freedom. The assimilation alternative is failing culturally even where it succeeds legally.
mechanism: Third internal diagnosis in three decades (Hess 1862, Pinsker 1882, Ahad Ha-Am 1891)
src: Ahad Ha-Am, 'Slavery in Freedom' (1891), in Selected Essays (Simon tr., JPS)

event: Ahad Ha-Am, "Truth from the Land of Israel" (second essay): First Aliyah colonists' conduct toward Arab neighbors documented by a Jewish primary — hostility, unjust encroachment, beatings, and boasting about it.
quote: והנם מתהלכים עם הערביים באיבה ואכזריות, משיגים גבולם שלא בצדק, מכים אותם בחרפה בלי כל סיבה מספקת, ומתפארים עוד כי כן יעשו. — "they behave toward the Arabs with hostility and cruelty, trespass unjustly, beat them shamefully for no sufficient reason, and even boast of it."
mechanism: Symmetric-rigor row: contemporaneous Jewish-primary attestation of Yishuv-side conduct
src: Ahad Ha-Am, 'Emet me-Eretz Yisrael' II, HaMelitz 1893 — Hebrew primary (Ben-Yehuda Project)
note: Original-language verification upgrades the Shapira-quoted rendering.

event: Herzl publishes Der Judenstaat (1896); the First Zionist Congress at Basel (Aug 1897) adopts "a home in Palestine secured by public law" — aspirational and deliberately ambiguous. Statehood does not become the mainstream movement's actionable demand for another 45 years.
mechanism: The eventual surviving form is articulated — but as one marginal option among the alternatives this ledger tracks
src: Framework §8 (late-formalization table); corpus: Herzl, Penslar
note: Political Zionism remained empirically marginal among Jews for decades: WZO shekel-payers at their 1939 peak were ~6–7% of world Jewry; American Zionist membership in 1918 was ~1.3% of American Jews (Urofsky).

event: The General Jewish Labour Bund is founded in Vilna: Jewish diaspora-socialism as a mass alternative. Into the late 1930s the Bund outpolls Zionist lists in major Polish kehilla elections (Warsaw, Łódź, 1938–39).
mechanism: Institutional vehicle: doikayt (hereness), Yiddish cultural autonomy, socialist politics in place
src: Framework §3 typology + §8 (kehilla elections); corpus: Slezkine

event: Territorialism: the Sixth Zionist Congress receives an actual British government territorial offer (the East Africa / "Uganda" scheme) and nearly splits over it; the Seventh Congress (1905) rejects it and Zangwill's Jewish Territorial Organization founds. The constituency is real: in the 1906 Russian-Jewish party landscape the territorialist SSRP out-organizes Poale Zion roughly 24,000 to 16,000, and the Brussels territorialist manifesto carries 294 signatures from inside the Yishuv itself.
actor: Zangwill; ITO; SSRP; British Colonial Office (the offer)
mechanism: A Jewish national territory somewhere other than Palestine — the four-part test met: real offer, mass constituency, organizational vehicle, plausible path
src: Vital, Zionism: The Formative Years (1982); Frankel, Prophecy and Politics (1981); conviction-page 1906 party table
note: Cross-link: the zionist-conviction page carries the 1906 party-membership table and the Brussels manifesto. Territorialism's entire viability rested on a willing host sovereign — the dependency that closes it (see its closure row and Évian).

event: Destination-preference and return-rate data: of 1,858 inquiry letters to the Hilfsverein bureau in 1906, 73% ask about the United States, 6% about Palestine. Jewish return-migration from the US runs at 5.2% — from Palestine, 75–80% (1905–07), still 51% by 1912–14.
quote: Of the 1,858 letters received in 1906… 73 percent contained requests for information about the United States… and only 6 percent about Palestine.
mechanism: Quantitative bedrock: Palestine was the low-preference, high-exit destination before the doors closed
src: Alroey, Bread to Eat and Clothes to Wear (2011), p. ~22; An Unpromising Land (2014), Table 6.3 (Hersch 1931)
note: Applies symmetrically in the framework: immigrant motivation data does not mitigate later Palestinian fear of the demographic effect — it locates the tragedy in interacting external closures.

event: Ottomanist autonomy: after the Young Turk revolution, a real current bets on a Jewish future inside the empire — Ben-Gurion and Ben-Zvi study Ottoman law in Istanbul planning careers in imperial politics; Ben-Gurion "considered himself an Ottoman patriot… He called the Ottoman Empire 'our country'… He thought of a Jewish national district within the Ottoman state"; HaShomer runs an Ottomanization current.
quote: He considered himself an Ottoman patriot… He called the Ottoman Empire 'our country'… He thought of a Jewish national district within the Ottoman state. Nor did he give up his dream of representing the Jewish public as a Turkish Cabinet minister. (Segev)
actor: Ben-Gurion; Ben-Zvi; post-1908 Ottomanist current in the Yishuv
mechanism: Autonomy-within-empire as the operative horizon — the man who became the state-builder was planning a future inside the Ottoman framework into WWI
src: Segev, A State at Any Cost (2019); Mandel, The Arabs and Zionism Before World War I (1976)

event: Ottoman parliamentary debate: a CUP official defends the government's handling of Zionist immigration on the ground that most European Jews, and all Ottoman Jews, "scoffed at the dreams of this group" — a "handful of charlatans" incapable of establishing a Jewish government in Palestine.
mechanism: Contemporaneous attestation that political Zionism was marginal — consistent with the preference and yerida data
src: Mandel, The Arabs and Zionism Before World War I (1976), p. 99 (PRO FO 371/1245/9105 + CZA Z2/11)
note: The same 1911 sessions carried the first Arab parliamentary anti-Zionist interpellations — while Ben-Gurion was studying Ottoman law in Istanbul planning a future inside the empire (Ottomanist-autonomy row).

event: The Yishuv's wartime near-destruction: from roughly 90,000 to under 60,000 through famine, disease, the deportation of enemy-subject Russian Jews, the forced evacuation of Jaffa–Tel Aviv (April 1917), and the Nili hangings — under a regime that had just demonstrated, on the Armenians, what it could do to a suspect minority concentrated in a strategic zone. Jamal Pasha's harsher instincts were checked contingently, by German and American pressure.
actor: Ottoman wartime regime (Jamal Pasha); famine and disease
mechanism: Wartime state coercion + subsistence collapse; minority survival again dependent on external-power pressure, not the local order
src: Segev, One Palestine, Complete (2000), Part I; standard estimates
note: The door of 1917 opened over a community that had barely survived the opening — the conjunction nearly failed at the substrate's moment of collapse. The halukkah-dependent Old Yishuv, cut off from diaspora remittances, starved worst.

event: Balfour Declaration, then the League Mandate: Britain undertakes to facilitate a Jewish "national home" and "close settlement on the land" (Article 6) while pledging that nothing prejudice the rights of the existing communities — and while denying the Arab majority self-determination. The contradiction is institutionalized, not resolved.
quote: The Administration of Palestine, while ensuring that the rights and position of other sections of the population are not prejudiced, shall facilitate Jewish immigration under suitable conditions and shall encourage… close settlement by Jews on the land.
mechanism: Incompatible expectations legitimated inside one legal container
src: Mandate for Palestine (1922), preamble + Article 6
note: The Cmd. 5974 committee (1939) later concluded the McMahon–Hussein correspondence could not settle whether Palestine had been promised to the Arabs — the incompatible-promises record ran back to 1915–16. Article 4 chartered one community's agency; the analogous Arab Agency, offered in 1923 on Balfour-bounded terms, was declined (see the 1922–23 row).

event: The Ottoman collapse (Mudros, Oct 1918 → San Remo, Apr 1920) — the largest double-sided foreclosure in the file. It closes Ottomanist autonomy at a stroke; and it strips the Arab side of its strongest structural protection: a retention-interested Muslim sovereign that had maintained a standing demographic veto (the Hamidian restrictions), replaced by a patron chartered to the Jewish national home.
actor: Allied powers; the dying Ottoman state
mechanism: Imperial death as substrate failure — slow enough to leak for forty years, then sudden enough to be replaced by a charter-bound patron rather than a consolidated successor
src: Framework §9 (every post-Ottoman successor formalized majority primacy; Palestine the chartered exception); Mandel (the demographic-veto record)
note: Removal test: no Ottoman collapse → the cap holds, the Yishuv plateaus as a capped millet, no charter ever exists — and after 1924 closes America, European Jewry faces the 1930s with no exit at all. Every other post-Ottoman successor state formalized the existing majority's primacy; San Remo chartered the opposite in one territory.

event: The Soviet path opens: Jewish Sections of the Communist Party (Yevsektsiya, 1918), then the Jewish Autonomous Oblast at Birobidzhan (1934) — Soviet universalism plus territorial autonomy as a state-sponsored alternative.
mechanism: State-sponsored institutional vehicle for Soviet Jews, 1917–48
src: Framework §3 typology; corpus: Slezkine

event: Nebi Musa riots, Jerusalem Old City: pogrom-like violence out of a religious procession — "Idbah al-Yahud" — six Jews dead, ~200 injured; British response "lackadaisical and inept." The Haganah is founded in response. The pre-war anti-civilian signal chain begins.
quote: A Muslim religious procession, the marchers wielding knives and clubs, erupted in anti-Jewish violence; shouts of 'Idbah al-Yahud' (Slaughter the Jews)… filled the air.
mechanism: Credibility signal, subtype A (anti-civilian targeting); first round of 1920 → 1921 → 1929 → 1936–39

event: Jaffa riots: 47 Jews and 48 Arabs killed (Haycraft Commission tally); the Jewish dead are predominantly mob victims, the Arab dead predominantly from British suppression fire — the commission's own analytical note.
quote: This gives a total of 95 killed — 48 Arabs and 47 Jews — and 219 wounded, of whom 73 were Arabs and 146 Jews.
mechanism: Credibility signal, subtype A — second round
src: Haycraft Commission, Cmd. 1540 (1921), §IX
note: Immigration is suspended in its wake — the first British use of the immigration lever under violence.

event: The XII Zionist Congress (Carlsbad) adopts the coexistence resolution: to live with the Arab people in friendship and mutual respect and develop the common homeland together. The movement's official position, on record via a British government report.
quote: solemnly declared the desire of the Jewish people to live with the Arab people in relations of friendship and mutual respect, and, together with the Arab people, to develop the homeland common to both into a prosperous community which would ensure the growth of the peoples.
mechanism: Documentary evidence against the 'always maximalist' reading; the coexistence strand was official, tried, and real
src: Carlsbad resolution, reproduced in Hope Simpson, Cmd. 3686 (1930)
note: Land-purchase and labor-exclusion practice diverged from the rhetoric (Hope Simpson row, 1930) — the divergence, not the absence, of the coexistence commitment is the finding.

event: Jabotinsky, "The Iron Wall": no voluntary Arab agreement to a Jewish-majority Palestine is possible; colonization can proceed only behind external protective power. A strategic hypothesis by one Zionist leader — later absorbed, in practice, by the mainstream he opposed.
quote: Zionist colonization can continue and develop only under the protection of a power that is independent of the native population, behind an iron wall, which the native population cannot break through.
mechanism: Strategic articulation of the external-guarantor dependency; treated as evidence of what one leader thought, not of how the system worked
src: Jabotinsky, 'The Iron Wall' (1923) — English ed. in corpus
note: Inventory reclassification note applies: a political-strategic essay, not a Mandate-commission or witness primary.

event: Churchill White Paper (Cmd. 1700) bounds the Balfour commitment: no "wholly Jewish Palestine," no "disappearance or subordination of the Arabic population"; the national home is the development of the existing Jewish community, gated by economic absorptive capacity.
quote: His Majesty's Government regard any such expectation as impracticable and have no such aim in view… not the imposition of a Jewish nationality upon the inhabitants of Palestine as a whole, but the further development of the existing Jewish community.
mechanism: First formal narrowing of the Balfour reading; the absorptive-capacity lever is installed

event: Majoritarian constitutionalism closes inside the Mandate frame — affirmatively, and from both sides. Britain offers only Balfour-bounded participation: the 1922 Legislative Council (8 Muslim, 2 Jewish, 2 Christian elected seats, national-home policy off the table) is boycotted — "the great majority of Arabs refused to vote"; the reconstituted Advisory Council collapses when acceptances are withdrawn under Arab Executive pressure; and the Arab Agency — "a position exactly analogous to that accorded to the Jewish Agency under Article 4" — is unanimously declined (Oct 1923). Constitutional participation was priced at accepting the Balfour framework; the Arab leadership declined participation at that price.
quote: a fully representative gathering of Arab leaders, who unanimously declined to accept it on the grounds that it 'would not satisfy the aspirations of the Arab people'.
actor: British government (Balfour-bounded offers); Arab Executive (refusal at that price)
mechanism: Legal-institutional closure, double-sided: the Mandate chartered one community's agency and barred elected majorities from the national-home question; the majority declined the bounded remainder
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I, ch. II, pp. ~21–22; Porath vol. 1
note: This upgrades the Arab-majority alternative from 'retrospective' to affirmatively foreclosed 1920–23 — a stronger Arab-side claim than the original grading. The Survey's editorial gloss ('the Arab objection was… to the whole policy of the Mandatory') is the Government's own framing and is flagged as such, per project discipline on Commission documents.

event: US Johnson-Reed Act cuts Southern/Eastern European immigration quotas by ~90%: the primary Jewish destination — the one preferred by ~73–80% of emigrants — is legally blocked. The dominant alternative begins its staged closure.
mechanism: Legal foreclosure of the primary destination; migration pressure re-channels (Fourth Aliyah begins within months)
src: Framework §2–3; Alroey (2014)
note: Severe narrowing, not total closure: Shanghai, partial UK, and partial Latin American routes remained (framework's own degree-of-closure discipline).

event: Fourth Aliyah (~82,000): the first restriction-channeled wave — Polish Grabski-era economic pressure plus the closed American door; ~15–20% ideologically Zionist by the corpus composition estimates.
mechanism: Demographic channeling: closed doors, not vanguard recruitment, set the flow
src: Framework stage 1 (subclaim.7 composition data); corpus: Alroey, Vital

event: Territorialism closes for want of a host sovereign: the East Africa offer lapses amid British settler opposition and the Seventh Congress rejection (1905); the Galveston channel ends with the war (1914); the ITO dissolves (1925); the Freeland League's late schemes (Kimberley, Suriname) fail. Every scheme required a willing sovereign — and sovereign willingness collapsed precisely when need peaked (Évian, 1938).
actor: Host governments (withdrawn willingness); Zionist Congress (1905 rejection)
mechanism: The same dependency as trusteeship later: paper schemes without a sovereign to enforce or host them
src: Vital, Zionism: The Formative Years (1982); Frankel, Prophecy and Politics (1981); Alroey
note: Évian 1938 is the terminal datapoint from another angle: 32 sovereigns asked directly, none willing. See the Évian row.

event: Joint Arab–Jewish labor organizing has a real institutional vehicle: the Histadrut-funded General Workers' Club opens in Arab Haifa (Khalfon and Hassun); the October 1925 carpenters' strike is its high point. The club declines from 1927 — economic downturn, nationalist and communist hostility, Histadrut budget cuts — and closes in 1928–29.
quote: In July 1925, with a small budget from the Histadrut, Khalfon and Hassun opened the 'General Workers' Club' in a busy, Arab, and largely Christian section of the 'old city' of Haifa.
mechanism: Actual constituency and vehicle — the four-part foreclosure test is met; decline begins before the 1929 violence
src: Lockman, Comrades and Enemies (1996), ch. 3, pp. ~94–100
note: Bidirectional causation held honestly: economic-structural pressures were already driving separation; 1929 completed rather than originated the closure.

event: Brit Shalom founded (Buber, Ruppin circle): Jewish-side binationalism acquires an institutional vehicle — a minority intellectual project, never mass politics.
mechanism: Institutional vehicle exists (1925–33); constituency remains thin on both sides
src: Framework §3 typology (Brit Shalom 1925–33)

event: The Wailing Wall / Buraq campaign: Husseini and the Supreme Muslim Council recode a bounded access dispute as a Jewish civilizational threat to al-Aqsa. Shaw finds he helped create societies to "mobilize Moslem opinion on the issue of the Wailing Wall" and bore "a share in the responsibility" — while finding no evidence of direct incitement to the August violence.
quote: the campaign of agitation waged by Amin al-Husayni and the SMC in 1928–9, which led to the outbreak of the Wailing Wall riots. (Porath, vol. 2, p. 49)
actor: Hajj Amin al-Husseini; Supreme Muslim Council
mechanism: Sacralization: bounded grievance → sacred-threat frame → mass mobilization → moderation becomes betrayal
src: Shaw Commission, Cmd. 3530 (1930); Porath, Palestinian Arab National Movement, vol. 2, p. 49
note: The Wall crisis was the one issue that overrode Arab factional divisions — which land sales never did (signal-register table, framework §8). Commission framings are themselves read against the corpus, per project discipline.

event: Countrywide massacres: 133 Jews killed, 339 wounded (87 Arabs killed, mostly by British suppression fire). At Hebron, 60+ dead — non-Zionist yeshiva students and families, killed by known neighbors with no military operation underway. The maximum-strength credibility signal: Ben-Gurion's question afterward — "Is it possible for us to exist here as long as we are a minority?"
quote: More than 60 Jews — including many women and children — were murdered and more than 50 were wounded. This savage attack, of which no condemnation could be too severe, was accompanied by wanton destruction and looting.
actor: Hebron/Safed mobs (mobilized via the sacral frame)
mechanism: Credibility foreclosure, subtype A at maximum strength: anti-civilian targeting of a combatant-free community signals that minority status is unsafe
src: Shaw Commission, Cmd. 3530 (1930); Shapira, Land and Power, pp. 174–175
note: Before 1929 Yishuv danger-perception was "limited, containable in predictable bounds" (Shapira). The Hebron Old Yishuv community — anti-Zionist, Haganah-protection-refusing — is destroyed: religious quietism loses its Palestine anchor. Arab neighbors sheltered ~250 Jews in the same event; the counter-current is carried in the defense-decoupling ledger.

event: Ben-Gurion reevaluates after August 1929: Palestinian Arab nationalism is no longer dismissed as an effendi fraud — and the doctrine that the Arab working class was Zionism's "natural ally" is abandoned. The strategic rationale for joint labor organizing is gone.
quote: This shift also implied abandonment of the notion… that the Arab working class was the Zionist project's natural (if not only) ally in the Arab community, and hence the loss of a prime ideological and strategic rationale for investing resources in organizing Arab workers.
mechanism: Strategic foreclosure downstream of the violence shock; organizational collapse directly traceable (Lockman)
src: Lockman, Comrades and Enemies (1996), ch. 2, pp. ~108–109
note: The framework's highest-confidence use of the verb "foreclosed" outside the hard-closure cases.

event: Philip Hassun — the Histadrut's Arab organizer in Haifa — is denounced in the nationalist press as "a lackey of the Jews and a traitor to his people." Arab participation in joint institutions is being reclassified as betrayal a decade before the Revolt makes the label lethal.
quote: As an Arab directly employed by the Histadrut and doing its work, Philip Hassun was a prime target of nationalist invective, denounced as a lackey of the Jews and a traitor to his people.
mechanism: Traitor-category weaponization — the reclassification that the 1936–39 assassination campaign will enforce physically
src: Lockman, Comrades and Enemies (1996), ch. 3, p. ~97

event: Statehood is still not the program: Ben-Gurion proposes a federation of cantons under British suzerainty (1929); WZO president Weizmann says demanding a Jewish state in Palestine "was like demanding one in Manhattan" (1930–31).
mechanism: Late-formalization evidence: autonomy-within-empire frameworks remain the mainstream horizon into the 1930s
src: Segev, A State at Any Cost (2019), pp. ~120, ~125

event: Hope Simpson (Cmd. 3686) documents the structural-dispossession channel: JNF land "extra-territorialised," the Arab cultivator "deprived for ever from employment on that land"; the Hebrew-labor boycott judged "contrary to Article 6… a constant and increasing source of danger." Passfield restricts; the MacDonald letter (1931) reverses. The Mandate zigzag radicalizes both sides.
quote: The principle of the persistent and deliberate boycott of Arab labour in the Zionist colonies is not only contrary to the provisions of that article of the Mandate, but it is in addition a constant and increasing source of danger to the country.
mechanism: Credibility foreclosure, subtype B (dispossession signals: land, labor, demography) — slower, structural, elite-mediated
src: Hope Simpson, Cmd. 3686 (Oct 1930), ch. VI
note: The Arab-side credibility channel documented by a British primary: rational fear of progressive displacement without any centralized expulsion plan.

event: The Irgun splits from the Haganah over restraint-versus-retaliation (1931); Lehi splits from the Irgun (1940). Rejection of defensive minimalism acquires permanent institutional form inside the Yishuv.
mechanism: Strategic foreclosure: the restraint doctrine loses its institutional monopoly under sustained attack
src: Framework §2–3; corpus: Shapira, Land and Power

event: Fifth Aliyah (~247,000) — the demographically decisive wave: Jewish population 175,000 → 460,000 (about 17% → 30% of Palestine) in six years; ~80–85% non-WZO-channeled, overwhelmingly Nazi-persecution refugees. Meanwhile the Palestine-share of German-Jewish emigration collapses — 42.6% (1934) to 12.0% (1938) — as British certificates tighten: even now Palestine is not the preferred door.
quote: [Lavsky Table IV — Palestine share of German Jewish emigration:] 1933: 20.5%; 1934: 42.6%; 1935: 41.0%; 1936: 34.8%; 1937: 16.1%; 1938: 12.0%.
actor: Refugees from Nazi Europe; British certificate policy
mechanism: Demographic foreclosure: closed doors elsewhere produce in Palestine the transformation that Palestinian politics rationally feared
src: Lavsky, Before Catastrophe (1996), Table IV, p. 252; framework stage 1 (subclaim.7)
note: Three claims held together (framework §8): the Palestinian fear tracked a real transformation; immigrant motivations don't change the effect; and for most of the immigrants the alternative was death. Two foreclosures interacting.

event: The Legislative Council proposal (Cmd. 5119): 28 seats allocated by community — the last pre-Revolt constitutional power-sharing design. Zionist leadership opposes it; Arab parties are divided but several are prepared to try it; Parliamentary criticism buries it. The constitutional channel closes months before the Revolt begins.
quote: The allotment of the seats in the Council as among elected members is based upon the numbers of the different communities in the total population of Palestine.
actor: British government; both communities' leaderships; Westminster
mechanism: Institutional foreclosure: the sole constitutional-sharing vehicle dies without replacement
src: Cmd. 5119 (March 1936, Wauchope statement Dec 1935)
note: Communal-proportional seat allocation shows British constitutional engineering formalizing segmentation rather than building a single demos.

event: The Arab Revolt's anti-Jewish dimension: Survey of Palestine year tables give 80 Jews killed in the 1936 disturbances, 255 in 1938 (peak), 94 in 1939; 1937 sees 438 bomb/firearm attacks, 143 against Jewish settlements. Five-source convergent range for Revolt-period Jewish dead: 429–547, in a distributed ambush-and-bombing pattern.
quote: 1938 (peak year): British 77 killed; Jews 255 killed; Arabs 503 killed… 'The number of Arab rebels killed by military and police action was conservatively estimated at not less than 1,000.'
mechanism: Credibility signal, subtype A, fourth round — distributed anti-civilian pattern over three years
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I, pp. 38–49
note: Arab casualties of the Revolt were several times higher (503 'terrorism' deaths in 1938 plus 1,000+ rebels killed by British action that year; ~3,000–4,000 total per Khalidi's chronology) — most at British hands, and roughly 900–1,000 in intra-Arab violence (next row).

event: The Revolt's intra-Arab war: rebel violence kills roughly 900–1,000 Arabs (Cohen's estimate, rejecting higher claims) — rivals, notables, land-sellers, labor leaders, mukhtars, policemen — under an elastic "collaborator" label. A Nablus oppositionist sees the pattern: a prominent opposition figure killed in each region of the country.
quote: they killed a prominent opposition figure in each of the country's regions: Rafe' al-Fahoum in Nazareth, Dr. Anwar Shuqayri in Acre, Ahmad and Muhammad Irsheid in Jenin, Hasan Sidqi al-Dajani in Jerusalem, Nassir al-Din Nassir al-Din in Hebron…
mechanism: Physical foreclosure by opposition-field decapitation: any Arab leader considering compromise must now assume he can be labeled a traitor and killed
src: Cohen, Army of Shadows (2008), p. 133 (Ihsan al-Nimer) and passim
note: Precisely scoped: this does not show a different leadership would have reached terms the Yishuv could accept; it shows the conditions under which Arab compromise politics could survive were destroyed. "Collaborator" is an emic accusation, not an analytic identity.

event: The Peel Commission (Cmd. 5479) recommends partition — with a compulsory-transfer clause modeled on the 1923 Greco-Turkish exchange: ~225,000 Arabs in the proposed Jewish state against ~1,250 Jews in the proposed Arab state. The AHC rejects partition outright; the Zionist Congress is deeply divided but negotiates.
quote: Sooner or later there should be a transfer of land and, as far as possible, an exchange of population… it is to be hoped that the Arab and the Jewish leaders might show the same high statesmanship as that of the Turks and the Greeks.
mechanism: First time partition/statehood is operationally live; transfer enters the record as a British recommendation
src: Peel Commission, Cmd. 5479 (July 1937), ch. XXII ¶35–42
note: Peel's own text concedes the Greco-Turkish precedent "manifestly imposed the gravest hardships on multitudes of people."

event: The Zionist transfer current consolidates under Peel: Weizmann to Ormsby-Gore, twelve days after publication — "the whole success of the scheme depended upon" transfer, which "could be carried out only by the British Government." Ben-Gurion, reading the report, underlines "compulsory transfer" in his diary; in 1938 he says "I favor forced transfer… but forced transfer is possible only by England."
quote: I said that the whole success of the scheme depended upon whether the Government genuinely did or did not wish to carry out this recommendation. The transfer could be carried out only by the British Government, and not by the Jews.
mechanism: Transfer-discourse consolidation: latent earlier (Herzl 1895 diary), operationally active only under the Peel/Revolt conjuncture
src: Weizmann–Ormsby-Gore memorandum, 19 July 1937 (Khalidi, Haven, Doc. 32); Segev (2019), pp. ~280–285
note: Symmetric-rigor row the thesis must own: 1937 Zionist acceptance was not pristine. Held with its context — the international 1930s consensus on population exchange (Shapira pp. 285–286) and the rapid walk-backs that follow (next rows).

event: The AHC's serial rejection pattern: Peel partition rejected (1937); even Woodhead's minimal Plan C — a small coastal Jewish state — rejected (1938); the 1939 White Paper rejected too, because it still admits 75,000 Jews. Across every proposal the constant is rejection of any Jewish collective national-political status, however small the territory.
mechanism: Structural-rejection pattern — the foreclosure was not an event but a demonstrated series
src: Framework stage 5 (Peel → Woodhead → White Paper → Morrison-Grady → UNSCOP → Res 181); corpus: Mattar, Porath vol. 2
note: Aggregate row. Read alongside the intra-Arab decapitation row: after 1936–39, no Arab institutional channel for negotiated response existed — the leadership that might have bargained was dead, exiled, or intimidated.

event: The transfer walk-back: HMG rejects compulsory transfer within five months of Peel (Cmd. 5634, Dec 1937); Woodhead (Cmd. 5854) then finds Plan A leaves 294,700 Arabs in the Jewish state against 7,200 Jews in the Arab state — a 41:1 asymmetry — and "no large scale voluntary transfer appears to us to be possible." Jewish opinion, Woodhead records, "would be opposed to the exercise of any degree of compulsion." Partition in its 1937 form is dead.
quote: His Majesty's Government had not accepted the Royal Commission's proposal for the compulsory transfer in the last resort of Arabs from the Jewish to the Arab area. On behalf of the Jews it was also made clear to us that Jewish opinion would be opposed to the exercise of any degree of compulsion.
mechanism: Demographic foreclosure made explicit: without compulsion the partition arithmetic fails; with it, Britain won't act
src: Cmd. 5634 (Dec 1937); Woodhead Commission, Cmd. 5854 (Nov 1938), ch. VIII ¶104–105
note: The operational opening Weizmann saw in July 1937 was closed by December 1937 — the walk-back is as much a part of the record as the current.

event: The Évian Conference: 32 countries meet on the refugee crisis; Roosevelt's own instruction is that additional Jewish immigrants be accepted "only within the annual quotas" — and the American position leads other delegations "to tighten rather than liberalise their offers of help." No country raises its quota.
quote: his instructions to the American delegates to the conference were that additional Jewish immigrants would be accepted in the U.S. but only within the annual quotas… the American emphasis on the immutability of the existing quotas influenced the other delegates to the conference to tighten rather than liberalise their offers of help.
mechanism: Legal/geopolitical foreclosure at the moment of maximum need — four months after the Anschluss
src: Khalidi, Introduction to From Haven to Conquest (1971), pp. xlvi–xlvii
note: The St. Louis (May–June 1939: 900+ refugees denied at Havana, turned back to Europe) is the emblem of the same closure. Évian is also territorialism's terminal datapoint: every territorialist scheme required a willing host sovereign, and here 32 sovereigns were asked directly at the moment of maximum need — none was willing.

event: The White Paper (Cmd. 6019): Britain states categorically that it is "not part of their policy that Palestine should become a Jewish state"; Jewish immigration capped at 75,000 over five years, all further immigration conditional on Arab acquiescence; land sales to be restricted by zone (the 1940 Land Transfer Regulations follow). Issued six months after Kristallnacht. The AHC rejects it as insufficient.
quote: The Government now stated categorically that this meant that it was 'not part of their policy that Palestine should become a Jewish state'… After these five years no more Jewish immigrants would be admitted 'unless the Arabs of Palestine are prepared to acquiesce in it.'
mechanism: Legal foreclosure of the rescue door at the moment of catastrophe + reversal of the Mandate bargain; fails both sides at once
src: Cmd. 6019 (May 1939), provisions via Barbour in Khalidi, Haven, Doc. 41
note: From the Jewish side, the Mandate bargain reversed at the moment of catastrophe; from the Arab side, too late and too little. Mandate cooperation is foreclosed as a framework for both.

event: The Arab-majority alternative is closed a second time — by its own leadership. The White Paper's constitutional head offers an independent Palestine State within ten years, with the Jewish population capped near one-third; "The former Arab Higher Committee, at the direction of the Mufti, rejected the terms of the White Paper but, on 29th May, the National Defence Party announced its readiness to co-operate with Government in giving effect to them." The current willing to say yes was the one the 1936–39 assassinations had broken.
quote: The former Arab Higher Committee, at the direction of the Mufti, rejected the terms of the White Paper but, on 29th May, the National Defence Party announced its readiness to co-operate with Government in giving effect to them.
actor: AHC (Mufti, from exile); National Defence Party (acceptance)
mechanism: Strategic self-closure — the offer's bearers reject the nearest thing to their own program that Britain ever put on paper
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I, ch. II, pp. ~52–54
note: Verb discipline: 'severely weakened,' not 'foreclosed' — the offer's deliverability was itself uncertain (the Survey: the constitutional proposals 'neither community had accepted'; war postponed the head entirely). Symmetric detail in the same source: the Jewish side answered the White Paper with its own campaign of attacks and sabotage through the summer of 1939. Morris weights this rejection heavily; the intra-Arab split (NDP acceptance) ties to the decapitation row.

event: The British refugee blockade: naval enforcement of the White Paper cap against refugee ships — Patria (Nov 1940, ~260 dead in the Haganah sabotage-gone-wrong), Struma (Feb 1942, turned back and sunk with one survivor) — continuing through the postwar detention camps at Cyprus.
mechanism: Legal + naval foreclosure of the last exit during the Holocaust
src: Framework §2–3 typology (British refugee blockade 1940–48)

event: The Farhud, Baghdad: pogrom against Baghdad's Jews during the collapse of the pro-Axis Rashid Ali government — ~180 dead by common estimates. Bears on the plausibility of Jewish minority-security fears under Arab-majority rule; not, by the framework's own scoping, direct evidence of any 1948 actor's intent.
mechanism: Minority-security failure mode visible in the region before 1948
src: Framework §8 (Mizrahi scoping note); corpus: Mandate/Mufti thread

event: The Holocaust physically destroys the constituencies of the European alternatives: assimilation, Bundism, and the ultra-Orthodox heartlands of religious quietism. Hard foreclosure — no actor could revive these in 1947 regardless of political will.
mechanism: Physical foreclosure at Level 1 of the closure hierarchy
src: Framework §3, §6 (Level 1)
note: The framework's degree discipline: these are the alternatives that fail the "could any advocate have revived this in 1947?" test absolutely.

event: The Biltmore Program demands a "Jewish commonwealth" as the war goal — the first mainstream actionable statehood demand, 45 years after Basel, mid-Holocaust, post-Struma, after the defense, refugee-absorption and labor infrastructures were already built. In the accompanying debate, agreement-based transfer is argued by Katznelson; Ben-Gurion in the 1940s opposes any imposed transfer plan.
quote: Its essential importance was that it presented a Jewish state in Palestine as the war goal of the Jewish people. (Shapira)
mechanism: The residue consolidates: statehood becomes the program only after the alternatives' closures have accumulated
src: Shapira, Land and Power (1992), pp. ~285–286
note: The WWII Jewish Agency memorandum explicitly rejected compulsory-transfer advocacy — the walk-back current is part of the same record (subclaim.9).

event: Ihud founded (Magnes, Buber): the last Jewish-side binational vehicle, formed against Biltmore — real advocates, minority position, no mass constituency.
mechanism: Political marginalization: the vehicle exists but never commands majority support on either side
src: Framework §3 typology (Ihud Association 1942)

event: Fawzi Darwish al-Husayni — a 1936 Revolt detainee turned binationalist — founds "The New Palestine": non-domination of either people, a binational state on political equality, Jewish immigration negotiable by absorptive capacity, UN confirmation, union with neighboring Arab states. Arab-side binationalism has a named platform and a leader.
quote: The condition for agreement is the principle of non-domination of one people by the other, and the establishment of a bi-national state based upon political equality and cooperation between both peoples in their economy, their social and cultural life.
mechanism: The four-part test met on the Arab side: real alternative, actual constituency, named vehicle, articulated path
src: Fawzi al-Husayni address (1946), quoted verbatim by Magnes in Goren ed., Dissenter in Zion (1982), p. 454

event: Fawzi al-Husayni is assassinated weeks after his platform. A quarter-century later Jamal al-Husseini says openly: "We bear responsibility for thirty to forty dead men, among them my cousin… we were compelled to send a man to kill him on his doorstep." The Arab-side binational current is physically eliminated.
quote: We acknowledge our responsibility. We carried out the attacks first and foremost to put an end to land sales… We bear responsibility for thirty to forty dead men, among them my cousin, whom we advised [to halt his actions] but who did not accept our advice, and we were compelled to send a man to kill him on his doorstep.
mechanism: Physical foreclosure — the late sequel to the 1936–39 decapitation, not an isolated act
src: Cohen, Army of Shadows (2008), p. 219 (Jamal al-Husseini, ~1971); Magnes (1947)
note: Cohen's care preserved: whether Fawzi was killed for land dealings or for his political contacts with Jews is not established — the elastic category covered both.

event: Sami Taha — Haifa head of the Palestine Arab Workers' Society, an Arab labor leader with a mass following and heterodox politics — is assassinated. Magnes, contemporaneously: "Despite the inner Arab terror, many thousands of Arabs from all walks of life attended his funeral."
quote: A few days ago a young Arab labor leader, Sami Taha, was assassinated. He and his considerable following had not been satisfied with the policies of the present Arab leadership. Despite the inner Arab terror, many thousands of Arabs from all walks of life attended his funeral.
mechanism: Physical foreclosure of the Arab labor-compromise stratum, ten weeks before the partition vote
src: Magnes (1947), in Goren ed., Dissenter in Zion (1982), p. 454
note: The funeral crowds are the constituency evidence: binationalism's Arab constituency existed and was being terrorized, not absent.

event: UNSCOP's minority plan (India, Iran, Yugoslavia): a single independent federal Palestine after a transitional period "not exceeding three years" under an authority chosen by the General Assembly — bicameral legislature with equal Arab-Jewish representation in one chamber, federal control of immigration, minority protections. The non-state path exists on paper — conditional on external administration.
quote: an independent federal State of Palestine shall be created following a transitional period not exceeding three years… responsibility for administering Palestine and preparing it for independence… shall be entrusted to such authority as may be decided upon by the General Assembly.
mechanism: The surviving non-state design — viable only with outside coercive force behind it
src: UNSCOP Report, A/364 (1947), vol. I, ch. VII

event: General Assembly Resolution 181: a non-binding recommendation of two states with minority-protection clauses and economic union. The Jewish Agency accepts; the AHC rejects it and offers no counter-partition. The resolution is never implemented — the 1949 lines are war-determined, not partition-determined.
mechanism: Partition-without-displacement is still theoretically live on 29 November — the last alternative standing, pending enforcement
src: GA Res 181 (II), 29 Nov 1947; framework §3 (wartime-conversion row)
note: Wording per project discipline: offer ≠ outcome; pre-war ownership and partition-internal allocations did not determine the territorial result — the war did.

event: Armed rejection begins the day after the vote: ambushes of two Jewish buses near Petah Tikva (~7 dead), a general strike, and the Jerusalem commercial-center riots open the civil war. The framework's terminal confirmation that no Arab institutional channel for negotiated response existed.
mechanism: Wartime conversion begins: the narrowed field will now be resolved by force
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), ~pp. 76ff; framework stage 5

event: The reprisal spiral in one 48-hour window: Irgun men bomb Arab workers at the Haifa refinery (~6 dead); Arab workers kill 39 Jewish co-workers inside; the Haganah's reprisal at Balad al-Shaykh kills roughly 60, including women and children. Categorical violence is now bidirectional and self-fueling.
mechanism: Tit-for-tat anti-civilian violence destroying residual intercommunal trust on both sides
note: Symmetric row by construction: three atrocities, three perpetrator sets, one mechanism.

event: Husseini-organized bombings of Jewish West Jerusalem: Palestine Post (1–2 Feb), Ben Yehuda Street (22 Feb — 58 dead, "almost all civilians"), the Jewish Agency compound (11 Mar — 12 dead). 71 civilian dead in six weeks, centrally organized.
quote: fifty-eight people died, almost all civilians, and thirty-two were seriously injured.
mechanism: Anti-civilian bombing campaign during the civil war phase

event: The UN Palestine Commission reports it cannot implement Resolution 181 "unless military forces in adequate strength are made available" — and records the AHC's refusal to recognize the resolution or "anything deriving therefrom": "not a single Arab will cooperate." The enforcement precondition for any non-state settlement is now explicit, and unmet.
quote: The Commission will be unable to establish security and maintain law and order… unless military forces in adequate strength are made available to the Commission when the responsibility for the administration of Palestine is transferred to it.
actor: UN Palestine Commission; Arab Higher Committee
mechanism: Institutional foreclosure: international authority without international force
src: UN Palestine Commission, S/676 (16 Feb 1948)
note: AHC communication, verbatim: partition will be resisted by force; the UN should abandon, not enforce, "such an injustice."

event: The last non-state path: the US proposes temporary UN trusteeship (Austin, 19 Mar; Truman, 25 Mar — "not… a substitute for the partition plan," "does not prejudice… the final political settlement"); a draft trusteeship agreement is tabled; State Department reporting (Kopper memo) records Arab-side willingness to consider unitary, federal or trusteeship forms with equal Senate representation and 100,000 immigrants. No member state offers troops. The special session ends as the Mandate expires.
quote: Unfortunately, it has become clear that the partition plan cannot be carried out at this time by peaceful means… With such a truce and such a trusteeship, a peaceful settlement is yet possible; without them, open warfare is just over the horizon.
actor: US government; UN Security Council / General Assembly
mechanism: The severe-narrowing case in its purest form: the alternative existed, was advocated at the highest level, and died for want of an army
src: Truman statement (25 Mar 1948); FRUS 1948 V/2 Docs 94, 105, 133; UNSC Res 44 (1 Apr 1948)
note: Kopper's memo is the evidence that late Arab-side diplomatic signaling included federal and minority-protection forms — not only majority rule with paper rights. What no signatory supplied was enforcement.

event: Deir Yassin: Irgun and Lehi forces kill ~100–120 villagers in a contested operation that exceeded any military necessity. The atrocity accelerates Palestinian flight countrywide and forecloses post-war alternatives — trust-based return and coexistence under Israeli authority — in the same signal register the pre-war chain had used.
mechanism: Wartime atrocity foreclosing post-war alternatives; on the framework's signal axis it differs from Hebron-class events (armed defenders, contested operation) — the Hiram row carries the closer analog
note: Temporal-register discipline: Yishuv wartime atrocities did not cause the pre-war foreclosure (the war was already its product); what they foreclosed was the post-war field.

event: The Hadassah medical convoy to Mount Scopus is ambushed and burned: 78 dead — doctors, nurses, academics, students, Haganah escorts — "many roasted alive." Morris: "The Arabs had had their revenge" (for Deir Yassin, four days earlier). Magnes, binationalism's Jewish anchor, is "in effect forced to quit" and leaves Palestine within days, never to return.
quote: By then, seventy-eight academics, doctors, students, nurses, and Haganah men were dead, many roasted alive… Hebrew University president Yehuda Leib Magnes, a pillar of the Ihud Association… was in effect forced to quit his job.
mechanism: Terminal event for Jewish-side elite binationalism; anti-civilian signal at maximum salience (marked medical convoy)
note: The spiral is explicit in the source: this was revenge for Deir Yassin, as Kfar Etzion's killers a month later would shout "Deir Yassin."

event: Kfar Etzion: after surrender, more than a hundred defenders are massacred — militiamen pouring in "shouting wildly 'Deir Yassin'" — the war's largest killing of surrendering fighters on either side. Some Legionnaires participate; others restrain and rescue. Load-bearing for the defeat-counterfactual: what surrender to irregulars looked like.
quote: When the photographer stopped taking pictures fire was opened up on us from all directions… A mass of Arabs poured into the settlements from all sides and attacked the men in the center of the settlement and in the outposts shouting wildly 'Deir Yassin.'
actor: Local militiamen; Arab Legion elements (mixed conduct)
mechanism: Counterfactual evidence (subclaim.8): defeat plausibly meant massacre where irregulars held the field
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), pp. 169–171; Knohl (1958) participant chronicle
note: Held with the next row (Jewish Quarter), which cuts the other way — the regular-army record is the qualifier the counterfactual must carry.

event: Britain withdraws without a successor regime: no cooperation with partition implementation, forces withdrawn area by area, no transitional authority constructed. "The vacuum was filled by armed conflict." The mediating structure that had contained the contradiction for thirty years is gone.
mechanism: Terminal institutional foreclosure — withdrawal of the container without a replacement
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), ~pp. 70–75; UNSCOP A/364 on British non-cooperation

event: Arab League armies invade. War-aims rhetoric in the invasion week: Azzam to Kirkbride — "It does not matter how many [Jews] there are. We will sweep them into the sea"; Quwwatli invokes the Crusades; Shukeiry, "the elimination of the Jewish state." Contextual constraint on the same leaders: Azzam had told Eban in September 1947 that Arab leaders "would probably be assassinated if they did nothing."
quote: It does not matter how many [Jews] there are. We will sweep them into the sea.
mechanism: Wartime conversion at full scale; rhetoric and operational record marked separately (see Jewish Quarter row)
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), p. 187 (FO 371/68403, Kirkbride) and p. 179 (Eban–Azzam)
note: The oft-cited Akhbar al-Yom "war of extermination" quote (11 Oct 1947) carries a disputed translation chain and is not laundered here: Morris himself chose the Kirkbride material. Rhetoric-maximalism and operational conduct are marked as separate axes (subclaim.8/11).

event: The Jewish Quarter of the Old City surrenders to the Arab Legion — and is not massacred. "The Legion had learned its lesson from Kfar Etzion": soldiers hold off the mob at gunpoint, carry stretchers, evacuate ~1,200 inhabitants to Jewish lines. Morris's summary: the Arab regular armies committed "few atrocities and no large-scale massacres" in the conventional war.
quote: We were all surprised by the Legion's behavior toward us… the Legion protected us even from the mob, they helped take out the wounded, they themselves carried the stretchers… their attitude was gracious and civil.
mechanism: Symmetric qualifier on the defeat-counterfactual: massacre risk tracked irregular-vs-regular control, not a uniform disposition
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), pp. 218–219, 405–406; Glubb, A Soldier with the Arabs (1957), pp. 129–130
note: Counter-current row retained, not buried: the strongest single piece of evidence against the maximal reading of subclaim.8, held in the open per project discipline.

event: Lydda and Ramle: Operation Dani ends with commander-level expulsion orders — roughly 50,000 people driven east, with ~250 killed in Lydda including at the Dahmash mosque. A choice within the narrowed field, and a foreclosure of the post-war field: return is now being physically pre-empted.
mechanism: Wartime operational decision foreclosing post-war return; constraint/choice/crime distinction applies in full
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), ch. on Dani; Morris, Birth… Revisited
note: The framework's Level-4 boundary: this is operationalization of the narrowed field, not the narrowing — and it is a crime within constraint, not a product of constraint alone.

event: The Israeli cabinet decides against refugee return during the war (16 June 1948), and the position hardens into policy as displacement reaches ~750,000 by the armistices. The post-war alternative of return is foreclosed by policy as well as by facts on the ground.
mechanism: Legal-policy foreclosure of the post-war field
src: Morris, Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited; framework stage 6

event: Operation Hiram and its aftermath in the Galilee: a cluster of massacres — Eilabun, Jish, 'Arab al-Mawasi, Saliha, Majd al-Kurum — "so late in the war, when the IDF was generally well disciplined and clearly victorious," tied by Morris to "general vengefulness and a desire by local commanders to precipitate a civilian exodus." The framework's Hebron-analog: killings in genuinely non-combat conditions, foreclosing Palestinian trust in Israeli-majority guarantees.
quote: This series of killings — at 'Eilabun, Jish, 'Arab al-Mawasi, Saliha, Majd al-Kurum, and so on — was apparently related to a general vengefulness and a desire by local commanders to precipitate a civilian exodus.
mechanism: Credibility foreclosure, subtype A, run in reverse: the symmetric entailment the framework must own
note: If anti-civilian targeting of non-combatants rationally destroys trust in minority-status arrangements, then Hiram — not Deir Yassin or Lydda, which involved contested operations — is the Hebron-class event on the Yishuv side, foreclosing trust-based return under Israeli sovereignty.

event: The conversion completed: ~750,000 Palestinians displaced by the armistices; the Yishuv's dead 5,700–5,800 (a quarter civilians, ~1% of the community); Yishuv troops "probably murdered some eight hundred civilians and prisoners of war all told." Atrocity arithmetic is threshold-dependent — Morris's strict 1948-war frame yields ~3:1 Yishuv-side; broader symmetric frames (1920–48 civilian dead) yield rough parity or uncertainty. The narrowed field has become territorial and demographic fact.
quote: In the yearlong war, Yishuv troops probably murdered some eight hundred civilians and prisoners of war all told… In the 1948 war, the Yishuv suffered 5,700–5,800 dead — one quarter of them civilians.
mechanism: Level-4 operationalization: displacement, statehood, territorial control, non-return
src: Morris, 1948 (2008), pp. ~398–406; Khalidi, All That Remains (1992) — its 13,000 aggregate is unfootnoted and flagged as such
note: Village-level detail lives in the companion 1948 depopulation ledger (376 events with Morris cause-codes). The three-way disambiguation of atrocity counts is subclaim.11.

event: The Soviet path closes: the Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee is dissolved and its leadership executed (Night of the Murdered Poets, Aug 1952); the anti-cosmopolitan campaign and the Doctors' Plot end Soviet universalism as a Jewish alternative. Corroborative, post-dating the 1948 outcome.
mechanism: Political-then-physical closure of the last diaspora-socialist vehicle
src: Framework §3 typology (anti-cosmopolitan campaign 1948–53)

event: Jewish communities across the Arab world — Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt and beyond — are expelled or driven out after 1948. In the framework's scoping: not a cause of Israeli state formation but retrospective corroboration of the minority-status failure mode visible before 1948, and regional-pattern evidence for Section 9.
mechanism: Corroborative regional pattern — the foreclosed alternative was Jewish minority security in an Arab-majority polity
src: Framework §8 (Mizrahi scoping) + §9; corpus: Laskier, Shvarts threads
note: Destination-preference caveat held symmetrically: even under expulsion pressure, many chose non-Israel destinations when available (Algerian 13:1 to France, 1962; post-1979 Iranians to the US). Treatment-after-arrival and pre-arrival motivation are independent axes.

event: The Mufti's consolidated retrospective doctrine, in his own name: the conflict is "a battle between two conflicting faiths, each of which can exist only on the ruins of the other"; "Reconciliation with the Jews is Suicidal for the Arab Nation." The sacralized, zero-sum frame stated as doctrine after the fact.
quote: Our battle with World Jewry… is a question of life and death, a battle between two conflicting faiths, each of which can exist only on the ruins of the other.
mechanism: Corroborative: the compromise-is-betrayal frame, from the actor who built it, in his own signed text
src: Husseini, Through the Eyes of the Mufti (Elpeleg ed., 2009), pp. 26, 125–126
note: Translation chain (Kessel-English ← Elpeleg-Hebrew ← al-Misri Arabic 1954) flagged per the inventory; the Arabic original should be consulted for any sharp lexical claim.
